title: Apologia adversus libros Rufini
author: Jerome
source: Translated by Claude from tmp424.tmp424.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Unde et Tul- lius in Commentariis causarum pro Gabinio : « Ego, inquit, cum omnes amicitias luendas sem- per putavi summa religione et fide, tum eas ma- xime quae essent ex inimicitiis revocatae in gratiam : propterea quod integris amicitiis officium praeter- missum, imprudentiae vel (ut gravius interprete- mur) negligentiae excusatione defenditur; post reditum in gratiam, si quid est commissum, id non neglectum, sed violatum putatur : nec im- prudentiae, sed perfidiae assignari solet. » Flaccus Horatius quoque in Epistola quam scribit ad Flo- rum : Male, ait, sarta Gratia nequidquam coit, et rescinditur.
passages.english: Hence Tullius too, in his Commentaries on cases, for Gabinius: "While I have always thought," he says, "that all friendships must be kept with the utmost scruple and good faith, [I have thought so] most of all of those which had been brought back into goodwill out of enmity; because in friendships that are unbroken, a duty neglected is defended by the excuse of thoughtlessness, or (to put it more severely) of negligence; but after a return to goodwill, if any fault is committed, it is thought not neglected but violated, and is usually ascribed not to thoughtlessness but to treachery." Horace Flaccus too, in the Epistle which he writes to Florus, says: "Goodwill badly patched closes up in vain, and is torn apart again."
passages.notes: "luendas" in the printed text is evidently a misreading of "colendas" ("to be kept/cultivated"); translated accordingly.

passages.original: Tu ad primum et solum opus, ignotus prius, temeritate factus es nobilis, Docet ipsa Praefatio, et Pamphili martyris librum pro defensione Origenis a te esse translatum. Et hoc agis totis viribus, ut cujus fidem martyr pro- bat, Ecclesia non refutet. Sex libros (ut ante jam dixi) Eusebius Caesariensis episcopus, Arianae quondam signifer factionis, pro Origene scripsit, latissimum et elaboratum opus; et multis testimo- niis approbavit, Origenem juxta se catholicum, id est juxta nos Arianum, esse, Horum tu primum librum vertis sub nomine martyris 2. Et miramur, si me homunculum parvi pretii, Origenis laudato- rem velis, cum martyri calumniam feceris?
passages.english: You, unknown before, became famous for rashness with your first and only work. The Preface itself shows that the book of Pamphilus the martyr in defence of Origen was also translated by you. And you strive with all your might to ensure that the Church should not reject one whose faith a martyr approves. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, once standard-bearer of the Arian faction, wrote (as I have said before) six books on behalf of Origen, a very extensive and elaborate work; and with many testimonies he proved that Origen was a catholic by his standard, that is, an Arian by ours. Of these you translate the first book under the name of the martyr. And do we wonder if you want me, a little man of small worth, [to be] a eulogist of Origen, when you have slandered a martyr?
passages.notes: The stray "2" after "martyris" is a footnote mark, omitted.

passages.original: hoc idem faciens in Apologia, quasi Pamphili, quod et in Origenis περ\ Αρχών translatione fecisti. Si iste Pamphili liber est, de sex libris quis erit primus Eusebii? In ipso volumine, quod tu Pamphili simulas, sequentium librorum facta mentio est. In secundo quoque et reliquis dicit Eusebius, quod in primo libro ante jam dixerat, et quod eadem repe- tere non debebat. Si totum opus Pamphili est, cur reliquos libros non transfers? Si alterius, cur no- men immutas? Taces; ipsae res loquuntur : vide- licet ut crederent martyri, 465 qui Arianorum principem detestaturi erant.
passages.english: doing the same in the Apology, supposedly Pamphilus', as you also did in the translation of Origen's Peri Archōn. If this is Pamphilus' book, which of the six books will be Eusebius' first? In the very volume which you pretend is Pamphilus', mention is made of the following books. In the second and the rest, too, Eusebius says what he had already said before in the first book, and that he ought not to repeat the same things. If the whole work is Pamphilus', why do you not translate the remaining books? If it is someone else's, why do you change the name? You are silent; the facts themselves speak: namely, so that those who would have abhorred the chief of the Arians might believe a martyr.
passages.notes: The "465" in the text is a page number from the printed edition, omitted.

passages.original: 10. Theophilus et Anastasius Origenem haereticum dicebant. — Defensor Origenis, et laudator Pam- phili, dicit Pamphilum nihil omnino scripsisse, nec proprii quidquam condidisse sermonis. Et hoc dicit jam Pamphilo martyrio coronato, ne habeas suffugium post editos ab Eusebio libros, hoc Pam- philum scripsisse.
passages.english: 10. Theophilus and Anastasius called Origen a heretic. — The defender of Origen and eulogist of Pamphilus says that Pamphilus wrote nothing at all and composed nothing in his own words. And he says this when Pamphilus had already been crowned with martyrdom, so that you may have no refuge [in claiming] that Pamphilus wrote this after the books published by Eusebius.
passages.notes: The subject is Eusebius ("defender of Origen and eulogist of Pamphilus"); the sense of the final clause is somewhat compressed.

passages.original: — Audio praeterea te quaedam de epistola mea philosophice carpere, et hominem rugosae frontis adductique supercilii, Plautino in me sale ludere, eo quod Barrabam Judaeum dixerim praeceptorem meum. Nec mirum si pro BAR-ANINA, ubi est aliqua vocabulorum similitudo, scripseris Barrabam, cum tantam ha- beas licentiam nominum immutandorum, ut de Eusebio Pamphilum, de haeretico martyrem feceris. Cavendus homo, et mihi maxime declinandus, ne me repente, dum nescio, de Hieronymo Sardana- palum nomines. Audi ergo, sapientiae columen, et norma Catonianae severitatis.
passages.english: — I hear, moreover, that you carp philosophically at certain things in my letter, and, a man of wrinkled forehead and knitted brow, make sport of me with Plautine wit, because I said that Barrabas the Jew was my teacher. No wonder if for Bar-Anina, where there is some similarity of names, you wrote Barrabas, when you have such licence in changing names that you have made Pamphilus out of Eusebius, a martyr out of a heretic. The man must be guarded against, and above all avoided by me, lest suddenly, without my knowing it, you call me Sardanapalus instead of Jerome. Hear then, pillar of wisdom and standard of Catonian severity.

passages.original: 14. Origenes damnatus. — Lectis nuper papae Theophili epistolis, in quibus Origenis exponit er- rores, dicitur obturasse aures suas, et auctorem tanti mali clara cum [Al. coram] omnibus voce damnasse 1, et dixisse, usque ad illud tempus se ignorasse, quod tam nefaria scripserit. Non recuso, nec dico quod alius diceret forsitan, non potuisse cum ignorare, quod interpretatus est, cujus Apologiam scriptam ab haeretico sub nomine martyris edidit : cujus defensionem etiam proprio volumine professus est : adversum quod in se- quentibus, si dictandi spatium fuerit, disputabo.
passages.english: 14. Origen condemned. — Having lately read the letters of Pope Theophilus, in which he sets out Origen's errors, he is said to have stopped his ears, and to have condemned the author of so great an evil with a loud voice before everyone, and to have said that until that time he had not known that he had written such wicked things. I do not object, nor do I say what another might perhaps say, that he could not have been ignorant of what he translated, of the man whose Apology, written by a heretic, he published under the name of a martyr, and whose defence he also professed in a volume of his own; against which I shall argue in what follows, if there is time for dictating.
passages.notes: "cum ignorare" read as "eum ignorare"; "[Al. coram]" is an editorial variant ("in the presence of"); the "1" is a footnote mark.

passages.original: Indignantur quare Origenistas scripserim in- ter se orgiis mendaciorum foederari. Nominavi librum, in quo hoc scriptum legerim : id est, sextum Stromateon Origenis, in quo Platonis sen- tentiae nostrum dogma componens, ita loquitur : « Plato in tertio de Republica libro : Veritas quo- que sectanda magnopere est. Si enim, ut paulo ante rectissime dicebamus, Deo indecens et inutile mendacium est, hominibus quandoque utile (ut utantur eo quasi condimento atque medicamine);
passages.english: They are indignant that I wrote that the Origenists are bound together among themselves by mysteries of lies. I named the book in which I had read this written: namely, the sixth book of Origen's Stromateis, in which, comparing our doctrine with the opinions of Plato, he speaks thus: "Plato in the third book of the Republic: Truth too must be pursued above all. For if, as we were saying very rightly a little earlier, falsehood is unbecoming and useless to God, but sometimes useful to men (so that they use it as a kind of seasoning and medicine);

passages.original: Vera, inquit, asseris : ergo principes urbium, si quibus et aliis hoc conceditur, oportet aliquando mentiri, vel contra hostes, vel pro patria et civibus. Ab aliis vero qui uti mendacio nesciunt, auferendum est omne mendacium. » Origenes : « Et nos igitur illius praecepti memores : « Loquimini veritatem unusquisque cum proximo suo (Ephes. IV, 25), » non debemus dicere, quis est proximus meus? sed considerare quomodo philosophus caute dixerit : Deo indecens et inutile esse mendacium, homini- bus interdum utile;
passages.english: You speak truly, he says: therefore the rulers of cities, if it is granted to any others as well, must sometimes lie, either against enemies or on behalf of the fatherland and the citizens. But from others, who do not know how to use falsehood, all falsehood must be taken away." Origen: "We therefore too, mindful of that precept, 'Speak the truth, each one with his neighbour' (Eph. 4:25), ought not to say, 'Who is my neighbour?' but consider how carefully the philosopher said that falsehood is unbecoming and useless to God, but sometimes useful to men;

passages.original: Didymus quoque et Apollinarius propria opuscula condidere. Quos ego vel transfe- rens, vel imitans, quid in Prologo ejusdem operis scripserim, subjiciam : « Illud quoque in Praefa- tione commoneo, ut sciatis Origenem tria volu- mina in hanc Epistolam conscripsisse, quem et nos ex parte secuti sumus : Apollinarium etiam et Didymum quosdam Commentariolos edidisse. Ex quibus licet pauca, decerpsimus; et nonnulla quae nobis videbantur, adjecimus sive subtraximus : ut studiosus statim in principio lector agnoscat, hoc opus vel alienum esse, vel nostrum (Prologus Comment.
passages.english: Didymus and Apollinarius also composed works of their own. Whom I either translating or imitating, I shall append what I wrote in the Prologue of that same work: "I also remind you in the Preface, so that you may know that Origen wrote three volumes on this Epistle, whom we too have followed in part; and that Apollinarius and Didymus also published certain short commentaries. From these we have culled, though only a few things, and have added or removed some things as seemed good to us, so that the studious reader may recognise right at the beginning that this work is either another's or ours (Prologue to the Commentary
passages.notes: The opening relative clause ("Quos ego vel transferens, vel imitans") is grammatically loose in the Latin, rendered literally.

passages.original: — ln primo statim volumine testimonium Pauli, in quo loquitur : « Sicut elegit nos in ipso ante constitu- tionem mundi : ut essemus sancti et immaculati coram ipso (Ephes.I, 4), » sic interpretati sumus, ut electionem non juxta Origenem eorum dicere- mus, qui prius fuerant; sed ad Dei praescientiam referremus. Denique diximus : « Quod autem ele- ctos nos, ut essemus sancti et immaculati coram ipso, hoc est, Deo, ante fabricam mundi, testatus est, ad praescientiam Dei pertinet, cui omnia futura jam facta sunt, et antequam fiant universa sunt nota.
passages.english: — In the very first volume, the text of Paul in which he says, "As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and spotless before him" (Eph. 1:4), we interpreted in such a way that we did not, following Origen, speak of the election of those who had existed before, but referred it to God's foreknowledge. Then we said: "That he has testified that we were chosen to be holy and spotless before him, that is, God, before the making of the world, belongs to the foreknowledge of God, to whom all future things are already done, and all things are known before they happen.

passages.original: 480 sin autem putat idcirco me Orige- nem sequi, quia profectus et honores, ascensiones et descensiones,, incrementa et immunitiones, in expositione mea posui; sciat multum in ter esse de angelis et Seraphim et Cherubim dicere, daemones et homines fieri, quod affirmat Origenes; et ipsos inter se angelos diversa officiorum genera osse sortitos, quod Ecclesiae non repugnat. Quomodo et inter homines ordo dignitatum ex laboris va- rietate diversus est, cum episcopus et presbyter, et omnis ecclesiasticus gradus habeat ordinem suum;
passages.english: But if he thinks that I follow Origen because I set down in my commentary advancements and honours, ascents and descents, increases and diminutions, let him know that there is a great difference between saying that from angels, Seraphim and Cherubim, demons and men come to be, which Origen asserts, and [saying] that the angels themselves have been allotted among themselves different kinds of offices, which is not contrary to the Church. Just as among men too the order of ranks differs according to the variety of labour, since bishop and presbyter and every ecclesiastical grade has its own order;
passages.notes: The opening '480' is a page number from the printed edition and has been omitted. 'immunitiones' is read as 'imminutiones' (diminutions), and 'osse' as 'esse'.

passages.original: Alii asserunt, quod, formatis in utero corporibus, Deus quotidie faciat animas et infundat. Alii quod 5 fa- ctas jam olim, id est, tunc cum omnia creavit Deus ex nihilo, nunc eas judicio suo nasci dispenset in corpore. Hoc sentit et Origenes et nonnulli alii Graecorum. Ego vero cum haec singula legerim (Deo teste dico) quia usque ad praesens certi et definiti aliquid de hac quaestione non teneo; sed Deo relin- quo scire quid sit in vero 6, et si cui ipse revelare dignabitur.
passages.english: Others assert that, once bodies have been formed in the womb, God makes souls daily and pours them in. Others [say] that, having been made long ago, that is, at the time when God created all things out of nothing, He now dispenses them by His judgement to be born in the body. This is the view of Origen and of some others among the Greeks. But as for me, though I have read each of these (I say it with God as witness), up to the present I hold nothing certain and settled on this question; rather I leave it to God to know what the truth is, and to anyone to whom He Himself shall deign to reveal it.
passages.notes: Jerome is quoting Rufinus's letter (to Anastasius). The words 'dico quia' are slightly awkward in the Latin; rendered as a simple statement.

passages.original: 9. Antequam de sensibus disputem, Theophrasti verba mirabor : « Audio, inquit, de anima quae- stiones commotas esse : de qua re utrum recipi debeat querimonia, aut abjici, vos probate.·» Si quaestiones de animae statu in Urbe commotae sunt, quae est ista querimonia vel querela, quae utrum recipi debeat, episcoporum judicio relinquitur?
passages.english: 9. Before I discuss the meaning, I will marvel at Theophrastus's words: "I hear," he says, "that questions have been stirred up concerning the soul: on which matter you must judge whether the complaint ought to be received or rejected." If questions about the state of the soul have been stirred up in the City, what is this complaint or grievance, whether it ought to be received being left to the judgement of the bishops?
passages.notes: 'Theophrastus' appears to be Jerome's mocking nickname for Rufinus (as a would-be fine speaker).

passages.original: 10. Trinitatis mysterium ignoratum antiquis. — O infelices animas, quae tantis vitiorum lan- ceis vulnerantur! non eas puto juxta Origenis errorem tantum laborasse, cum de coelo in terras ruerent, et crassis corporibus vestirentur, ut nunc et verbis et sententiis hino inde collisas : ut prae- termittam χχκέμφατον1 quo de humani seminis traduce diffundi animae dicuntur.
passages.english: 10. The mystery of the Trinity unknown to the ancients. — O unhappy souls, wounded by such great lances of faults! I do not think that, according to Origen's error, they toiled as much when they fell from heaven to earth and were clothed with gross bodies, as [they do] now, battered on this side and that by words and by meanings: to pass over the indecent expression by which souls are said to be diffused through the transmission of human seed.
passages.notes: The Greek 'χχκέμφατον' is a scanning corruption of κακέμφατον (an ill-sounding or indecent expression). 'hino' read as 'hinc'. The section heading does not match the content of this passage.

passages.original: In primo libro iup\ Αρχών, ubi Origenes lingua sacrilega blasphema- vit, quod Filius Patrem non videat, tu etiam causas reddis, quasi ex persona ejus, qui scripsit, et Didymi interpretaris (??)2, in quo ille casso labore conatur alienum errorem defendere, quod Origenes quidem bene dixerit : sed nos simplices homines, et cicures Enniani 3, nec illius sapientiam, nec tuam, qui interpretatus es, intelligere possu- mus. Praefatio tua, quam nominas, et in qua me miris ornas laudibus, te reum pessimae transla- tionis facit.
passages.english: In the first book of the Peri Archōn, where Origen with sacrilegious tongue blasphemed that the Son does not see the Father, you even supply reasons, as if in the person of the one who wrote, and you translate the scholion of Didymus, in which he strives with empty labour to defend another's error, [claiming] that Origen indeed spoke well, but we simple men, Ennius's 'tame folk', can understand neither his wisdom nor yours, who translated [it]. Your preface, as you call it, in which you adorn me with wonderful praises, makes you guilty of a most wicked translation.
passages.notes: 'iup\ Αρχών' is a corruption of Περὶ Ἀρχῶν. A Greek word after 'Didymi' is lost in the scan (marked (??)); probably σχόλιον, 'scholion'. 'cicures Enniani' alludes to a phrase of Ennius.

passages.original: 15. Rufinus Origenis defensor probatur. Eusebius Arianorum princeps. Rufini praefatio in Apologiam Pamphili pro Origene. — Dicis te non esse defen- sorem neque assertorem Origenis : jam nunc tibi proferam librum tuum de quo in famosa illa prae- fatiuncula praeclari operis tui his verbis loqueris : « Cujus diversitatis causam plenius tibi in Apolo- getico, quem Pamphilus in libris suis scripsit, edidimus brevissimo libello superaddito, in quo exidentibus, ut arbitror, probamentis, corruptos esse in quamplurimis ab haereticis et malevolis libros ejus ostendimus, et praecipue istos, quos nunc exigis ut interpreter, id est, (??) 'Αρχών.
passages.english: 15. Rufinus is proved a defender of Origen. Eusebius chief of the Arians. Rufinus's preface to Pamphilus's Apology for Origen. — You say that you are not a defender or champion of Origen: I will now bring forward your own book, about which you speak in these words in that notorious little preface to your splendid work: "The cause of this inconsistency I have set out more fully for you in the Apology which Pamphilus wrote in his books, adding a very short treatise in which, by evident proofs, as I think, I have shown that his books have been corrupted in very many places by heretics and malicious persons, and especially these which you now require me to translate, that is, the Peri Archōn."
passages.notes: 'exidentibus' read as 'evidentibus'. A Greek word is lost before 'Αρχών', evidently Περὶ.

passages.original: » Quamvis de Eusebii libro multa subtraxerit, et in bonam partem de Filio et Spiritu sancto nisus sit commutare; tamen multa in illo scandala reperiuntur, et apertissimae bla- sphemiae, quae iste sua negare non poterit, catho- lica esse pronuntians. Dicit Eusebius, imo (ut tu vis) Pamphilus, in isto volumine, Filium Patris ministrum 2 : Spiritum sanctum non de eadem Patrie Filiique substantia : animas hominum lapsas esse de coelo : et in hoc quod sumus de angelis commutati, in restitutione omnium aequales et angelos, et daemones, et homines fore;
passages.english: Although he removed much from Eusebius's book and tried to change [statements] about the Son and the Holy Spirit in a good sense, nevertheless many stumbling-blocks are found in it, and the most open blasphemies, which he will not be able to deny are his own, since he declares them catholic. Eusebius, or rather (as you will have it) Pamphilus, says in that volume that the Son is the minister of the Father; that the Holy Spirit is not of the same substance as the Father and the Son; that the souls of men fell from heaven, and that in what we are we were changed from angels; that in the restoration of all things angels, demons and men will be equal;
passages.notes: 'Patrie' read as 'Patris'.

passages.original: Vir doctissimus Eusebius (doctissimum dixi, non catholicum, ne, more solito, mihi et in hoc ca- lumniam struas) per sex volumina nihil aliud agit, nisi ut Origenem suae ostendat fidei, id est, Arianae perfidiae. Et multa ponit exempla, et hoc constan- ter probat. Tibi ergo in quo somnio Alexandrini carceris revelatum est, ut quae ille vera profitetur, falsata contingas?
passages.english: That most learned man Eusebius (I said most learned, not catholic, so that you may not, as usual, contrive a slander against me in this too) through six volumes does nothing else but show that Origen was of his own faith, that is, of Arian faithlessness. And he sets out many examples and proves this consistently. In what dream of the Alexandrian prison, then, was it revealed to you that you should claim to be falsified what he professes to be true?
passages.notes: 'contingas' read as 'confingas'. The 'Alexandrian prison' presumably alludes to some episode in Rufinus's life.

passages.original: » Clementem quoque Alexandrinae Ecclesiae presby- terum, virum catholicum, scribit in libris suis interdum Det Filium dicere creatum, et Dionysium Alexandrinae urbis episcopum, virum cruditissi- mum, contra Sabellium quatuor voluminibus dis- putat tem, in Arianum dogma delabi. Et sub his exemplis illud agit, ut non ecclesiasticos et ca- tholicos viros male sensisse, sed ab haereticis eo- rum scripta corrupta esse testetur, et concludat ad extremum, dicens : « De Origene quoque, in quo similiter, ut in his quos supra diximus, quae- dam diversitas invenitur, istud non sufficiat sen- tire, quod de praejudicatis jam catholicis sentitur vel intelligitur viris, ne simili causae, similis sufficiat excusatio.
passages.english: "He also writes that Clement, presbyter of the Alexandrian Church, a catholic man, in his books sometimes says the Son of God was created; and that Dionysius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, a most learned man, while arguing against Sabellius in four volumes, slips into the Arian doctrine." And under these examples his aim is to testify not that churchmen and catholic men thought wrongly, but that their writings were corrupted by heretics; and he concludes at the end, saying: "Concerning Origen too, in whom, as in those we mentioned above, a certain inconsistency is found, let it not suffice to think what is thought or understood about men already adjudged catholic, lest for a similar case a similar excuse should not suffice."
passages.notes: 'Det' read as 'Dei', 'cruditissimum' as 'eruditissimum', 'disputat tem' as 'disputantem'. The final clause ('ne ... sufficiat') is awkward as transmitted; the sense may require 'non sufficiat' or similar.

passages.original: Si tihi diceretur, quos habet Origenes in haeresi socios, recte ista proferes. Nunc a te quaeritur, haec quae in Origenis libris scripta reperiuntur, bona sint an mala? Taces, et pro his alia loqueris. Clemens hoc ait, Dionysius in isto errore deprehenditur : Athanasius [Al. Anastasius] episcopus 5 sic Diony- sii defendit errorem : apostolorum scripta similiter depravata sunt; quomodo et nunc ab aliis tibi haereseos crimen impingitur, et tu pro te taces et pro me confiteris.
passages.english: If you were asked whom Origen has as companions in heresy, you would rightly bring these things forward. Now you are asked whether these things which are found written in Origen's books are good or bad. You are silent, and in their place you speak of other things. Clement says this, Dionysius is caught in that error, Bishop Athanasius thus defends Dionysius's error, the writings of the apostles were similarly corrupted; just as now the charge of heresy is thrust upon you by others, and you are silent on your own behalf and confess on mine.
passages.notes: A variant reading gives 'Anastasius' for 'Athanasius'. 'tihi' read as 'tibi'.

passages.original: 18. Epistola Origenis ad amicos Alexandriae. Origenianae epistolae prior pars. — Praemissa falsatione ab haereticis, apostolorum, et utriusque Clementis, atque Dionysii, venit ad Origenem, et his verbis loquitur : « Ipsius hoc conquerentis et deplorantis scriptis ac vocibus probavimus. Quid enim ipse cum adhuc in carne vivens 1, sentiens, vidensque perpessus sit de librorum suorum vel sermonum corruptionibus, vel adulterinis edilio- nibus, ex ipsius epistola quam scribit ad quosdam charos suos Alexandriam, evidenter docetur.
passages.english: 18. The letter of Origen to his friends at Alexandria. The first part of Origen's letter. — Having first set out the falsification [of writings] by heretics, [those] of the apostles, and of both Clements, and of Dionysius, he comes to Origen and speaks in these words: "We have proved this from the writings and words of the man himself, complaining and lamenting it. For what he himself suffered while still living in the flesh, aware of it and seeing it, concerning the corruptions of his books or sermons, or spurious editions, is clearly shown from his own letter which he writes to certain dear friends of his at Alexandria.
passages.notes: The "1" after "carne vivens" is a footnote mark and has been omitted.

passages.original: Habetur dialogus apud Graecos Origenis et Candidi Valentinianae haereseos defen- soris, in quo duos Andabatas digladiantes inter se spectasse me fateor. Dicit Candidus Filium de Patris esse substantia, errans in eo quod προβο- λήν1, id est, prolationem asserit. E regione Ori- genes juxta Arium et Eunomium repugnat, eum vel prolatum esse, vel natum, ne Deus Pater dividatur in partes; sed dicit sublimem et excel- lentissimam creaturam voluntate exstitisse Patris, sicut et caeteras creaturas.
passages.english: Among the Greeks there is a dialogue between Origen and Candidus, a defender of the Valentinian heresy, in which I confess I have watched two *andabatae* [gladiators who fought blindfolded] fighting each other. Candidus says that the Son is of the substance of the Father, erring in this, that he asserts a *probolē*, that is, an emission. On the other side Origen, in agreement with Arius and Eunomius, denies that He was either emitted or born, lest God the Father be divided into parts; but he says that [the Son] came into being as a sublime and most excellent creature by the will of the Father, just as the other creatures also did.
passages.notes: The footnote mark '1' after προβολήν has been omitted, and words split by line breaks have been rejoined. 'Repugnat, eum vel prolatum esse, vel natum' is compressed: Origen objects to [the claim] that the Son was emitted or born. Andabatae were gladiators who fought in helmets without eye-holes, so the image is of two combatants fighting blind.

passages.original: Asserit Candidus diabolum pessimae esse naturae, et quae salvari nunquam possit. Contra hoc recte Origenes respondit, non cum periturae esse substantiae, sed voluntate pro- pria corruisse, et posse salvari. Hoc Candidus vertit in calumniam, quasi Origenes dixerit, diaboli naturam esse salvandam : quod ille falso obje- cerat, hic refutat. Et intelligimus in hoc tantum dialogo ab Origene argui haereticam falsitatem, et non in caeteris libris, de quibus nunquam quaestio fuit.
passages.english: Candidus asserts that the devil is of a most evil nature, and one that can never be saved. Against this Origen rightly answered that he is not of a substance destined to perish, but fell by his own will, and can be saved. Candidus turns this into a slander, as though Origen had said that the devil's nature is to be saved: what the one had falsely objected, the other refutes. And we understand that in this dialogue alone a heretical falsification is charged by Origen, and not in his other books, about which there was never any question.
passages.notes: "non cum" read as "non eum" (scanning error).

passages.original: Alioqui si omnia quae haeretica sunt, non erunt Origenis, sed haereticorum : omnes autem prope- modum illius tomi his erroribus pleni sunt : nihil Origenis erit, sed eorum, quorum ignoramus vo- cabula. Non ei sufficit Graecos et antiquos calum- niari, de quibus pro vetustate temporum et lon- ginquitate regionum habet licentiam quidquid voluerit mentiendi : venit ad Latinos, et primum ponit Hilarium 2 confessorem, quod post Arimi- nensem synodum liber 513 illius falsatus ab hae- reticis sit. Et ob hanc causam cum in concilio episcoporum ei quaestio moveretur, proferri librum de domo sua jusserit : qui, nesciente se, in scriniis suis haereticus tenebatur.
passages.english: Otherwise, if everything that is heretical is not Origen's but the heretics', and almost all his volumes are full of these errors, nothing will be Origen's, but [the work] of those whose names we do not know. It is not enough for him to slander the Greeks and the ancients, about whom, because of the remoteness of the times and the distance of the regions, he has licence to lie as much as he likes: he comes to the Latins, and first puts forward Hilary the confessor, [claiming] that after the synod of Ariminum a book of his was falsified by heretics; and that for this reason, when a question was raised against him in a council of bishops, he ordered the book to be brought from his house; and that, without his knowing it, it was being kept in his book-cases in heretical form.
passages.notes: "513" is a page number of the printed edition and has been omitted, as has the footnote mark "2".

passages.original: Nihil horum nominas, sed virum eloquentissimum, et contra Arianos Latini sermonis tubam, ut Origenem defendas, excommu- nicatum a synodo criminaris. Sed confessoris calumnia utcunque toleranda est. Transit ad inclytum martyrem Cyprianum, et dicit Tertulliani librum, cui titulus est, de Trinitate, sub nomine ejus Constantinopoli a Macedonianae partis haere- ticis lectitari. In quo crimine mentitur duo. Nam nec Tertulliani 3 liber est, nec Cypriani dicitur;
passages.english: You name none of these things, but, in order to defend Origen, you accuse of having been excommunicated by a synod a most eloquent man, the trumpet of the Latin tongue against the Arians. But the slander against a confessor is somehow to be tolerated. He passes on to the renowned martyr Cyprian, and says that a book of Tertullian entitled On the Trinity is read under his name at Constantinople by heretics of the Macedonian party. In this charge he tells two lies. For the book is neither Tertullian's, nor is it said to be Cyprian's;

passages.original: Et superfluum puto apertas ineptias confutare, cum mihi mea ingeratur fabella, a synodo videlicet 4, et sub nomine cujusdam amici Damasi Romanae urbis episcopi ego petar, cui ille ecclesiasticas epistolas dictandas tradidit, et Apollinariorum versutiae describantur, quod Athanasii librum ubi Dominicus homo scriptus est, ad 514 legendum acceptum ita corruperint, ut in litura id quod raserint, rursus scriberent, ut scilicet non ab illis falsatum, sel a me additum putaretur.
passages.english: And I think it superfluous to refute obvious absurdities, when my own little tale is thrust upon me — from a synod, no less — and I am attacked under the name of a certain friend of Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, to whom he entrusted the dictation of church letters; and the craftiness of the Apollinarians is described, how, having received for reading a book of Athanasius in which the phrase "the Lord's man" was written, they so corrupted it that they wrote again over the erasure what they had scraped off, so that it would be thought to have been not falsified by them but added by me.
passages.notes: "sel" read as "sed"; "514" is a page number.

passages.original: Non enim possibile est, tam iniquo judicio uti quemquam hominum, ut de causa aequali non aequaliter sentiat. Sed quod auctores obtrectatorum ejus hi sunt, qui vel in Ecclesia disputare latius solent, vel etiam libros scribere, qui totum de Origene vel loquuntur, vel scribunt. Ne ergo plures ipsorum furta cognoscant, quae utique si ingrati in magistrum non essent, nequaquam criminosa viderentur, simpliciores quosque ab ejus lectione deterrent. Denique quidam ex ipsis, qui se velut evangelizandi necessitatem per omnes gentes et per omnes linguas habere putat, de Origene male loquendi, sex millia librorum ejus se legisse, quam plurima 515 fratrum mul- titudine audiente, confessus est.
passages.english: "For it is not possible for any human being to use so unjust a judgement as not to judge equally in an equal case. But [the truth is] that the instigators of his detractors are those who are accustomed either to discourse at length in church, or even to write books, which they both speak and write entirely from Origen. So, lest more people discover their thefts — which, if they were not ungrateful to their master, would by no means seem criminal — they deter all the simpler folk from reading him. Finally, one of them, who thinks he has, as it were, a necessity laid on him of preaching through all nations and in all languages — of speaking ill of Origen — confessed, in the hearing of a very great multitude of brothers, that he had read six thousand of his books.
passages.notes: Jerome is quoting Rufinus's Apology. "515" is a page number.

passages.original: 22. Epiphanius quinque linguas noverat. — Qui sunt isti, qui in Ecclesia disputare latius solent? qui libros scribere? qui totum de Origene toquun- tur et scribunt? qui dum sua nolunt furta cognosci, et ingrati sunt in magistrum, idcirco simplices ab illius lectione deterrent? Nominatim debes dicere, et ipsos homines denotare. Ergo beati episcopi Anastasius 3, et Theophilus, et Venerius (Medio- lani), et Chromatius (Aquileiae), et omnis tam Orientis quam Occidentis Catholicorum synodus 4, qui pari sententia, quia pari et spiritu, illum hae- reticum denuntiant populis, fures librorum illius judicandi sunt : et quando in Ecclesiis praedicant, non Scripturarum mysteria, sed Origenis furta commemorant?
passages.english: 22. Epiphanius knew five languages. — Who are these who are accustomed to discourse at length in church? who write books? who speak and write entirely from Origen? who, because they do not want their thefts known and are ungrateful to their master, therefore deter the simple from reading him? You ought to say [it] by name and point out the men themselves. So then the blessed bishops Anastasius, and Theophilus, and Venerius (of Milan), and Chromatius (of Aquileia), and the whole synod of Catholics both of the East and of the West, who with one judgement, because with one spirit, denounce him to the peoples as a heretic, are to be judged thieves of his books? And when they preach in the churches, do they recount not the mysteries of the Scriptures but the thefts from Origen?
passages.notes: Footnote marks omitted.

passages.original: eruditus], et ab infantia sacris Litteris institutus, pro curiositate et scientia le- gisset aliena. Quod vero ille non scripsit, quomodo iste legere potuit? Numera indices librorum ejus qui in tertio volumine Eusebii, in quo scripsit vi- tam Pamphili, continentur : et non dico sex mil- lia, sed tertiam partem nou reperies. Habemus epistolam supradicti pontificis, in qua huic calum- niae tuae, dum adhuc esses in Oriente, respondet, et apertissimum mendacium libera veritatis fronte confutat.
passages.english: learned], and instructed from infancy in the sacred Scriptures, had read others' works out of curiosity and for knowledge. But how could he read what Origen did not write? Count the lists of his books contained in the third volume of Eusebius, in which he wrote the life of Pamphilus: and you will find, I do not say six thousand, but not a third of that. We have a letter of the aforementioned bishop in which he answers this slander of yours while you were still in the East, and refutes a most open lie with the free countenance of truth.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence after an editorial variant note "[Al. ..." (alternative reading) whose opening lies in the preceding context.

passages.original: Nunc tantum tuis assertionibus obviasse sufficiat, et hoc breviter prudentem instruxisse le- ctorem, me istum librum qui sub nomine Pamphili ferebatur, vidisse primum scriptum in codice tuo; et quia non erat mihi curae quid pro haeretico di- ceretur, sic semper habuisse, quasi diversum esset opus Pamphili et Eusebii : postea vero quaestione mota, scriptis eorum respondere voluisse, et ob hanc causam legisse, quid pro Origene unusquisque sentiret, perspicueque deprehendisse, quod primus liber sex voluminum Eusebii ipse esset, qui unus sub nomine Pamphili a te editus est, tam Graece quam Latine, immutatis duntaxat sensibus de Fi lio et Spiritu sancto, qui apertam blasphemiam praeferebant.
passages.english: For now let it suffice to have met your assertions, and briefly to have informed the prudent reader of this: that I first saw this book, which was circulated under the name of Pamphilus, written in your manuscript; and because I did not care what was said on behalf of a heretic, I always regarded it as though the work of Pamphilus and that of Eusebius were different; but later, when the controversy arose, I wished to reply to their writings, and for this reason read what each thought on behalf of Origen, and clearly discovered that the first book of Eusebius's six volumes was the very one that was published by you as a single book under the name of Pamphilus, in Greek as well as in Latin, with only the statements about the Son and the Holy Spirit altered, which displayed open blasphemy.

passages.original: 24. Epistola supposita Hieronymo. — Scribit fra- ter Eusebius se apud Afros episcopos, qui propter ecclesiasticas causas ad comitatum veneram, epi- stolam quasi meo scriptam nomine repetisse, in qua agerem poenitentiam, et me ab Hebraeis in adolescentia inductum esse testarer, ut Hehraea volumina in Latinum verterem, in quibus nulla sit veritas.
passages.english: 24. A letter forged in Jerome's name. — Brother Eusebius writes that among the African bishops who had come to the court on church business he had found a letter written as if in my name, in which I did penance and testified that in my youth I had been induced by the Hebrews to translate Hebrew books into Latin in which there is no truth.
passages.notes: "repetisse" read as "reperisse"; "veneram" read as "venerant".

passages.original: Si nondum emendatae, nec ad purum digestae erant schedulae, error earum non Eusebio imputabitur, sed mone et tarditati tuae, qui emendare cessasti. Et in eo solo erit iile culpa- bilis, quia scripta tua cito disseminavit in vulgus, quae tu paulatim emendare decreveras. Sin autem, ut tu vis, eas falsavit Eusebius : quid causaris, arque praetendis inemendatas, et necdum ad purum digestas in publicum prorupisse? Et emendatae enim, et non emendatae similem recipiunt falsita- tem. Nullus, inquis, eos habebat libros, aut ad- modum pauci.
passages.english: If the sheets had not yet been corrected or put into clean order, their error will be charged not to Eusebius but to your delay and slowness, since you failed to correct them. And he will be blameworthy in this alone, that he quickly spread among the public your writings, which you had decided to correct little by little. But if, as you would have it, Eusebius falsified them, why do you complain and plead that they burst out into public uncorrected and not yet put into clean order? For corrected and uncorrected alike admit the same falsification. "No one," you say, "had those books, or very few."
passages.notes: "mone" read as "morae" (delay); "iile" as "ille"; "arque" as "atque".

passages.original: 12. Ridiculosa res et ridicula, Fides Romana prae- stigias non recepit. — De Pamphili libro, non ridi- culosa, ut tu scribis, sed ridicula mihi forte res accidit, ut postquam Eusebii asseruerim esse, non Pamphili, ad extremum dixerim, etiam me annos plurimos hoc putasse, quod Pamphili fuerit, et a te exemplar hujus voluminis mutuatum. Vide quan- tum timeam cachinnos tuos, ut etiam nunc eadem ingeram.
passages.english: 12. A laughable thing and a ridiculous one; the Roman faith has not accepted the trickery. — Concerning the book of Pamphilus, a thing not laughable, as you write, but perhaps ridiculous happened to me: that after I had asserted it was Eusebius's, not Pamphilus's, I said at the end that I too had for very many years thought it was Pamphilus's, and that I had borrowed a copy of this volume from you. See how much I fear your guffaws, that even now I press the same points on you.
passages.notes: The opening is a section heading in the edition; Jerome plays on Rufinus's distinction between "ridiculosa" and "ridicula".

passages.original: Non tibi sufficit scandalum Grae- ciae, nisi illud et Latinorum auribus ingeras, et inclytum martyrem tua quantum in te est trans- latione deformes. Tu quidem alia mente fecisti, non ut me accusares, sed ut Origenis per nos scripta defenderes. Attamen scito Romanam fidem, apostolica voce laudatam, istiusmodi praestigia non recipere : etiam si angelus aliter annuntiet, quam semel praedicatum est, Pauli auctoritate munitam non posse mutari.
passages.english: It is not enough for you to have caused scandal in Greece unless you also press it upon the ears of the Latins and, as far as lies in you, disfigure an illustrious martyr by your translation. You indeed did it with another intention, not to accuse me, but to defend through me the writings of Origen. Yet know that the Roman faith, praised by the apostle's voice, does not accept trickery of this kind: even if an angel should announce otherwise than has once been preached, [that faith], fortified by the authority of Paul, cannot be changed.

passages.original: Tu qui per singulas paginas fumos meos ventilas, non intel- ligis videre nos caligines tuas et turbines? Nam ut tibi sciolus esse videaris, et apud Calpurnianos 1 discipulos doctrinae gloriam teneas, totam mihi physicam opponis, ut frustra Socrates ad ethicam transiens dixerit : Quae supra nos, nihil ad nos. Ergo nisi tibi rationem reddidero : quare formica parvum animal, et punctum, ut ita dicam, corpo- ris, sex pedes habeat, cum elephantis tanta moles quatuor pedibus incedat;
passages.english: You who on every page fan my smoke, do you not understand that we see your fogs and whirlwinds? For in order to seem learned to yourself, and to keep a reputation for scholarship among your Calpurnian disciples, you set the whole of natural science against me, so that Socrates said in vain, when he turned to ethics: "What is above us is nothing to us." So, unless I give you an account of why the ant, a small animal and, so to speak, a mere dot of a body, has six feet, while the elephant, so great a mass, walks on four feet;
passages.notes: The footnote mark '1' after 'Calpurnianos' has been omitted. 'Calpurnianos' is probably a contemptuous nickname for Rufinus' followers; its reference is uncertain. The sentence continues in the following passage.

passages.original: 29. Naturales quaestiones. — Urges ut respon- deam de natura rerum. Si esset locus, possem tibi vel Lucretii opiniones juxta Epicurum, vel Ari- stotelis juxta Peripateticos, vel Platonis atque Ze- nonis secundum Academicos et Stoicos dicere, Et ut ad Ecclesiam transeam, ubi norma est veritatis, multa et Genesis et Prophetarum libri ac Eccle- siastes nobis de hujuscemodi quaestionibus sug- gerunt.
passages.english: 29. Questions of nature. — You press me to answer concerning the nature of things. If there were room, I could tell you the opinions either of Lucretius following Epicurus, or of Aristotle following the Peripatetics, or of Plato and Zeno according to the Academics and Stoics. And to pass over to the Church, where the rule of truth is, the books of Genesis and of the Prophets and Ecclesiastes suggest to us many things about questions of this kind.
passages.notes: The opening is a section heading in the edition.

passages.original: Et iterum cla- mitas, et Aquileiae atque Alexandriae te didicisse jactas, quod sit Deus et animarum et corporum creator. De hoc scilicet quaestio ventilatur, utrum Deus an diabolus animas fecerit; et non utrum animae ante corpora fuerint, quod vult Origenes, et egerint aliquid, propter quod sint crassis cor- poribus alligatae : an in morem glirium torpentes consopitaeque dormierint. Haec taces, quae omnes flagitant : et ad illa respondes, quae nullus in- quirit.
passages.english: And again you shout, and boast that you learned at Aquileia and Alexandria that God is the creator both of souls and of bodies. As if, of course, the question being aired were whether God or the devil made souls, and not whether souls existed before bodies, as Origen holds, and did something on account of which they have been bound to gross bodies, or whether, torpid and lulled like dormice, they slept. These things you pass over in silence, which everyone demands; and you answer those things which no one asks.

passages.original: Non ut tu calumniaris et fingis, in Pythagorae et Platonis et Empedoclis libris, sed quae in illis fuisse legeram, et aliorum me scripta eos habuisse docuerunt. Et hoc genus elocutionis frequentissi mum est : ut si dicam, quae in Socrate legi dogmata, putavi vera. Non quod Socrates libros ullos scri- pserit 2; sed quae legi apud Platonem et alios So- craticos illum habuisse. Et rursum, imitari volui gesta quae in Alexandro et Scipione legeram : non quod ipsa sua gesta descripserint, sed quod apud alios legerim, quae illos gessisse mirabar.
passages.english: Not, as you slanderously pretend, [things] in the books of Pythagoras and Plato and Empedocles, but what I had read were in them, and what the writings of others taught me they had held. And this kind of expression is very common: as if I should say, "The doctrines I read in Socrates I thought true." Not that Socrates wrote any books, but [I mean the doctrines] which I read in Plato and other Socratics that he held. And again: "I wanted to imitate the deeds I had read in Alexander and Scipio"; not that they themselves wrote down their own deeds, but that I read in others the things I admired them for having done.
